extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; legislators and moralists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria for what counts as moral virtue, how virtues are acquired and tested, and how actions should be evaluated (voluntary/involuntary, mean between excess and defect, relation to pleasure/pain, role of reason/practical wisdom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition by habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues are acquired by repeatedly performing the relevant actions (e.g., by doing just actions we come to be just; by building one becomes a builder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the arts: instructors and law-givers train people by habituation; without practice no one becomes virtuous merely by talk. Examples: harp-players learn by playing; builders by building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions precede and produce virtues (practice-first requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing single acts of working precedes and produces the stable state (virtue); one is not virtuous merely by occasionally performing right acts unless done in the manner of the virtuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To possess virtue one must do actions 'as the just and self‑mastering do them' — i.e., knowingly, with deliberate choice for the things' own sake, and stably (not by chance or external suggestion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to pleasures and pains (object-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Virtue has for its object-matter pleasures and pains because pleasure often motivates wrong action and pain can deter right action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue consists in receiving right impressions of pleasure and pain; training should aim to make persons take pleasure/pain from proper objects. Punishments, remedies, and education operate via pleasure/pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of habit formation: affective endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign that a habit/virtue is formed is the pleasure or pain accompanying the action: the self‑mastering person abstains and is glad to do so; the brave man faces danger with pleasure or without pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mere outward compliance (abstaining with regret) from genuine virtue (abstaining with approval or absence of pain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is a state (not mere feeling or capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue belongs to the class of 'States' (dispositions) rather than Feelings (emotions) or Capacities: it disposes a person to feel and act rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feelings and capacities alone do not make one good or bad; virtues are stable dispositions that regulate feelings and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean between excess and defect (doctrine of the mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtue is a relative mean between two vices, one of excess and one of defect, aiming at the right amount, person, time, object, and manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples mapped: courage (mean) between rashness (excess) and cowardice (defect); liberality between prodigality and stinginess. The mean is praised; extremes are blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean is relative (person-sensitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct mean is not an absolute arithmetical midpoint but relative to the individual and circumstances (what is 'right' differs for Milo and a novice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical judgment must account for the individual's capacities and situation; one aims at the mean 'relative to ourselves' rather than a single universal measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination by Right Reason and Practical Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean is determined by Reason and by the judgment of the practically wise person (phronimos); virtue is 'determined by reason, and as the man of practical wisdom would determine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract general maxims are insufficient; right application to particulars requires practical wisdom. The text accepts 'act in accordance with Right Reason' as a basic maxim to be explicated later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate choice and stability as requisites for true virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: To truly possess a virtue one must act knowingly, with deliberate preference for the good for its own sake, and be stable (not apt to change); knowledge alone is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with arts: for virtues, besides knowledge, deliberate preference and stability are 'all in all'. Mere occasional right acts (by chance) do not constitute virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some acts intrinsically wrong (no mean applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain feelings and actions (e.g., malevolence, shamelessness, adultery, theft, homicide) are intrinsically bad and cannot be made right by finding a mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For such cases there is no excess/defect/mean calculus: any instance of these actions is wrong; the doctrine of the mean does not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical specification requirement (right particulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Right action requires getting particulars right: for whom, when, why, how long, and in what manner to feel or act (e.g., how to feel anger appropriately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rules are necessarily vague; moral perception ('Moral Sense') and practical wisdom must judge borderline degrees and particulars. Small deviations may be excused; large ones incur blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment rule: avoid the extreme more contrary to the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: When aiming at the mean, one should guard most against the extreme that is more opposed to the mean (choose the lesser of two evils if uncertain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: consider your natural biases (often toward pleasure) and steer away from the more contrary extreme; sometimes over-correct toward the opposite side to reach the mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological criterion: virtue makes one perform one's function well
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence (virtue) makes the agent good and enables him to perform his proper work well (analogy with eye, horse, artisan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue is defined by its contribution to good functioning; moral excellence is the aptness to aim at the mean so as to perform human function well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness as ground for praise/blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise and blame attach to voluntary actions; involuntary actions (due to compulsion or ignorance) may excuse the agent and attract allowance or compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action is compulsory if origination is external and the agent contributes nothing. Actions from ignorance are not automatically involuntary—only those attended with pain and remorse count as truly involuntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed actions (duress/choice interplay) evaluated by proximate origination
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done under pressure or for greater evils can be 'mixed'—they are often choice-worthy in the particular circumstance and thus judged more like voluntary actions because origination of motion rests with the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: throwing goods overboard to save lives; obeying orders to save family. Such acts may be praised, blamed, or merely excused depending on ends and motives; evaluate by immediate choice and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective bias and practical correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Human bias toward pleasures makes one prone to certain extremes (e.g., lack of self-control); thus moral training must take account of natural biases and deliberately correct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical methods: force oneself in the contrary direction (like straightening bent timber), guard carefully against pleasure, and adopt the safest plan by avoiding the more contrary extreme.
